column1: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
column2: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years later, and the Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her.
column3: Ancient Egypt was already ancient to the ancient Egyptians.

column1: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
column2: Teaching at Oxford was underway by 1096. The Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
column3: Old and "new" world timelines overlap in surprising ways.

column1: The shortest war lasted under an hour
column2: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment. The Sultan's palace was wrecked and a pro-British ruler installed.
column3: Power gaps can make conflicts brutally brief.

column1: Napoleon was not unusually short
column2: He was about 5 feet 7 inches, average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth grew from confusion between French and English inches and from British cartoons mocking him.
column3: Propaganda can outlive the person it targets.

column1: The Great Fire of London had few recorded deaths
column2: The 1666 fire destroyed around 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the true toll among the poor was higher but went uncounted.
column3: Who gets counted shapes what history remembers.

column1: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
column2: No horned helmet has been found from a Viking-age warrior grave. The image comes largely from 19th-century art and costume design, including Wagner's opera productions.
column3: Much of our picture of the past is Victorian stagecraft.

column1: The printing press spread faster than you would think
column2: Gutenberg printed his Bible around 1455. By 1500, presses operated in more than 250 European towns and had produced millions of books.
column3: New information technology has always spread fast.

column1: Ancient Romans used a kind of concrete that lasts
column2: Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash. Some harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of seawater, and researchers think minerals growing inside the concrete help seal cracks.
column3: Old techniques can still teach modern engineers.

column1: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
column2: The conflict between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453. It was a series of wars broken by truces, not one continuous fight.
column3: Historians name periods after the fact, not neatly.

column1: Tsar Peter the Great taxed beards
column2: In 1698 Peter imposed a tax on beards to push Russian nobles towards Western European fashion. Payers carried a token proving they had paid.
column3: Rulers have long used taxes to change behaviour.

column1: The Black Death killed around a third of Europe
column2: Between 1347 and 1351 plague swept Europe, killing an estimated 30 to 50 percent of the population. Labour shortages afterwards pushed up wages for surviving workers.
column3: Catastrophes can shift economic power.

column1: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary
column2: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it had a 20-year permit. It was saved partly because it proved useful as a radio transmission tower.
column3: Usefulness is a strong defence against demolition.

column1: Ancient Olympians competed naked
column2: In the ancient Greek Games, male athletes competed nude. The word "gymnasium" comes from the Greek "gymnos", meaning naked.
column3: Words carry fossils of old customs.

column1: The Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs
column2: Found in 1799, the stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek. Jean-François Champollion used it to announce his decipherment in 1822.
column3: One translated text can open a whole lost language.

column1: Mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built
column2: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid was built around 4,500 years ago.
column3: Extinction is often a slow fade, not a single event.

column1: The first known strike was in ancient Egypt
column2: Around 1157 BC, tomb builders at Deir el-Medina stopped work because their grain rations were late. Records of the protest survive on papyrus.
column3: Workers have bargained over pay for over 3,000 years.

column1: The Library of Alexandria declined slowly
column2: There was no single fire that destroyed everything. The library faded over centuries through funding cuts, political purges and several conflicts.
column3: Institutions usually die from neglect, not drama.

column1: Sliced bread was briefly banned in the US
column2: In January 1943 the US banned sliced bread to save resources during the war. Public outcry got the ban lifted within about two months.
column3: Small comforts can carry big political weight.

column1: Medieval people did not think the Earth was flat
column2: Educated Europeans in the Middle Ages generally knew the Earth was round. The flat-Earth myth about them was popularised in the 1800s.
column3: Each era likes to think the last was more ignorant.

column1: The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon
column2: It is very long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts have confirmed it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
column3: Big claims deserve a quick check.

column1: Coffee houses were nicknamed penny universities
column2: In 17th-century England, a penny bought entry and coffee, plus hours of debate and news. Lloyd's of London began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house.
column3: Shared spaces can incubate whole industries.

column1: Paper money started in China
column2: China was using paper money by the Song dynasty in the 11th century. Europe did not adopt banknotes widely until the 1600s.
column3: Many "modern" inventions are centuries old.

column1: The Titanic's sister ship had a long career
column2: RMS Olympic, Titanic's near-identical sister, served from 1911 to 1935. She was nicknamed "Old Reliable" and even rammed a German U-boat in 1918.
column3: Fame often goes to the disaster, not the success.

column1: The Aztec capital was built on a lake
column2: Tenochtitlan stood on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways. Mexico City sits on the drained lakebed and is sinking as a result.
column3: Cities inherit the choices of their founders.

column1: The Romans had fast food counters
column2: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, street counters serving hot food and drink. Many Romans in cramped flats had no kitchen of their own.
column3: Eating out is as old as city living.
